The Battle of the Kura River took place in 1265, between the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate. The battle was fought along the banks of the Kura River, the engagement was a critical moment in the Berke–Hulagu war. The Golden Horde emerged victorious, a result that allowed them to exert control over much of Azerbaijan for a perioud.

Background
The roots of the battle lay in a bitter personal and political feud between Berke Khan and his cousin Hulagu Khan. While both were grandsons of Genghis Khan, they disagreed sharply over the management of the Empire. Berke, a devout Muslim, was particularly incensed by Hulagu’s destruction of Baghdad and the execution of the Caliph. When Hulagu died in early 1265, Berke saw the succession of the young Abaqa Khan as the perfect opportunity to strike and reclaim disputed lands in the Caucasus.
Battle
Under the command of the fierce general Nogai Khan, the Golden Horde’s vanguard pushed south through the Caucasus passes. They were met at the Kura River by an Ilkhanid force initially led by Abaqa’s brother, Yushumut.
The fighting was intense and characterized by the fast-moving horse archery typical of Mongol warfare. During the heat of the combat, Nogai Khan was struck in the eye by an arrow—an injury that would leave him partially blinded for the rest of his life but cemented his reputation for toughness. Despite this blow to their commander, the Golden Horde’s riders managed to overwhelm the Ilkhanid lines, forcing Abaqa’s troops to pull back across the river.
Aftermath
In the wake of their victory, the Golden Horde occupied large sections of Azerbaijan, securing valuable grazing lands and trade routes. However, their hold on the region was fragile. The rugged geography of the Caucasus made it difficult to keep the army supplied from the north. When Berke Khan himself died unexpectedly in 1266 while preparing a follow-up campaign, the momentum of the invasion collapsed, and his forces eventually withdrew. The Kura River remained a tense and bloody border between the two powers for generations.
